intelligence.essence: Bounded Recovery Liveness Law: NayaNET may claim bounded recovery liveness only where obligation eligibility, scheduling opportunities, usable service, progress witnesses, capacity assumptions, and the governing bound are independently established. A finite timeout may demonstrate a specific contractual deadline breach, but shall not by itself establish weak- or strong-fairness failure. Safety holds remain authoritative; liveness machinery may require investigation, service or governed escalation but may never manufacture execution permission or successful completion. The operational behavior: 'This task timed out, but that alone does not prove unfair scheduling. I will determine whether it was genuinely executable, whether it received usable service, and whether a verified recovery milestone was owed within a qualified bound. I will escalate the specific failure that the evidence establishes — without weakening the safety boundary.' That gives NayaNET something much stronger than a timeout alarm: a reproducible, independently verifiable explanation of whether recovery was legitimately waiting, unfairly starved, inadequately executed, or actually completed.
intelligence.falsifier: A single timeout labeled a fairness violation; elapsed wall-clock standing in for eligible opportunities; DISPATCHED counted as SERVICED without resource evidence; a heartbeat counted as progress; a numeric bound enforced without proven capacity/scheduling assumptions; one collapsed timer replacing eligible-service age and total unresolved age; an escalation that manufactures permission; a 'repaired' claim from a consumed retry budget with the objective still unresolved.

human_view.meaning: A timeout is not a verdict — it's a question. The law answers it with evidence: was the task genuinely executable, did it receive usable service, was a verified milestone actually owed within a proven bound? Four claims stay separate forever: that nothing unsafe happened, that eligible work got fair service, that service produced real progress in time, and that the original objective actually succeeded — each needs its own proof. Three observable links per obligation: enabled (LAW permits, dependencies ready, resources available, no safety hold), serviced (lease, acknowledgment, actually usable resources — a scheduler claiming dispatch is not enough), progressed (a proof obligation discharged or a governed disposition reached — a heartbeat is not progress). Three different bounds: how quickly eligible work must receive service, how quickly serviced work must produce a verified milestone, how quickly an unresolved obligation must reach a governed disposition — and disposition is not completion; timely escalation with the objective still open is a valid bounded outcome. The worked example makes it concrete: six rounds, a timeout in round five, verified progress in round six — service PASS, progress PASS, no fairness violation; change one fact (service never arrives) and the third eligible opportunity without service becomes a proven bounded-service breach — still not a weak/strong fairness violation. No bound is real until its assumptions are proven: finite queue, correct scheduler, genuine opportunities, accurate accounting, usable service, restart continuity, no hidden unbounded delays. A task outstanding 30 minutes with 29 minutes of verified provider outage is not a scheduler failure; a task ignored across hundreds of fast eligible rounds in two seconds can breach its bound before any five-minute alert fires — hence both eligible-service age and total unresolved age, always. The verdict ladder climbs only as evidence permits: timeout observed, waiting authority, insufficient evidence, starvation suspected, then — only with a complete independently verified trace — bounded-service or bounded-progress violation, then formal fairness counterexamples, then governed disposition. Every claimed violation ships a ten-field evidence packet a cold verifier can replay. Twelve adversarial fixtures, crowned by the paired experiment: CONTROL and TREATMENT with identical timeout timestamps — one legitimately waiting on authority, one starved by a defective scheduler — and the detector must tell them apart, then survive the mutation that counts dispatch as service.
